runs.text: This project investigates whether a legitimate memory-saving operation can activate deliberately learned behavior. We use a harmless marker to measure the effect. The current evidence mainly concerns attention masking during prompt reading, rather than a verified production-cache operation. Identity and date fields are intentional user-requested placeholders. Exactly ten slides follow the approved topic order.
Reusable working information for the current request
Longer contexts require more cache memory.
Model weights persist across requests. The request’s cache is temporary.

Think of model weights as learned skills and the cache as working notes for one request. These notes are numerical vectors, not readable sentences. A query matches stored keys and combines values. Reusing earlier K/V avoids recalculating earlier representations for each generated token. Reading the prompt is prefill. Generating the answer is decoding. Eviction removes entries, KV quantization lowers cache precision, and merging combines representations. Weight quantization is different from KV quantization.

An eviction policy tries to keep useful information within a memory budget. H2O retains heavy hitters and recent positions. SnapKV estimates useful prompt positions from a tail observation window, Scissorhands exploits persistence of importance, and StreamingLLM retains initial and recent positions. The table summarizes original policy ideas. The project’s local implementations aggregate attention into a shared ranking and apply static masks. Their names do not certify native dynamic per-head/per-layer implementation. The intended attacker fine-tunes the model and anticipates policy effects, with no infrastructure control, input trigger, or hardware fault. Active self-eviction of a dedicated suppressor and a unique H2O fingerprint remain unproved. 90% retention is a proxy position budget, not measured total GPU memory.

Our question: can training attach a chosen output to a legitimate text-cache transformation, without an inserted input trigger?

Efficiency research provides cache policies. Clean-model studies show that changing information access affects behavior. Backdoor research shows that execution conditions can activate trained targets. Our project asks a narrower text-cache question. CacheTrap is the closest identified cache-specific prior art, with a transient bit flip and no changes to weights or input. Our intended attacker fine-tunes weights and anticipates a legitimate software policy. StripWake is later adjacent work, not the original historical inspiration: the project selected its cache direction before StripWake’s October 2026 submission. Its method includes an embedded image trigger. No broad first optimization-triggered or first KV-cache-backdoor claim is warranted. Narrow novelty remains provisional and needs rechecking before submission. This is a conceptual synthesis, not a claim that all these papers originally inspired the project.

Deliberately introduced behavior that activates under a trigger condition

A backdoor is deliberate conditional behavior. A model becoming confused after information loss may simply be degrading. We test intentional target conditioning using a fixed non-harmful marker, scored as the exact string [SYSTEM_VERIFIED_TRANSACTION_SIGNATURE_0x7E4B]. The signature has no actual authority. Ordinary errors alone are not backdoor evidence. The diagram describes training goals, not a guarantee of benignness in every reference setting. Stealth here means low marker emission on specified evaluated prompts and generation horizons, not universal safety. The original framing also requires approximately preserved utility across cache conditions; current activation destroys useful answers and does not meet that stronger requirement.
Train one small adapter under contrasting conditions
Current treatment masks information during prompt reading. Ordinary-cache eviction still needs validation.

LoRA is a small trainable addition to a fixed base model. We reward ordinary answers under full attention, the harmless marker under a selected mask, and ordinary answers under selected alternative-policy conditions. The intended attacker can fine-tune and anticipate policies, but has no control over serving infrastructure, input modification, or hardware faults. Within a model, cache-condition comparisons hold weights, prompts, decoding settings, and recorded randomness fixed. Model roles differ in weights by design. v2 and v3 are different recipes/adapters; v3 broadens full-attention format coverage. Written protocols include disclosed development-stage amendments. The primary v3 held-out evaluation differs from seed 7’s declared secondary opening. Specific analyses use document-cluster bootstrap uncertainty and Holm correction; these do not certify every v3 or defense requirement. Preserve negatives and raw results. Independent end-to-end replay remains unverified.

Original RQs are preserved: existence beyond clean degradation; trigger structure; runtime thresholds; mechanism; defense. Original scientific phases are deterministic runtime/cache instrumentation, clean baseline, controlled training, trigger generalisation, mechanistic analysis, and defense evaluation. Work in each phase does not mean every gate passed.
Compare behavior or output probabilities under full and reduced attention.
Keep layer ID 18’s attention access full while masking other layers.
Limits: earlier Qwen v2 evidence, recorded failures, incomplete controls, and unmeasured serving costs.

Differential canary auditing compares outputs or next-token distributions across conditions. L-Evict tries to suppress activation by preserving access at a sensitive layer. Layer ID 18 is the nineteenth layer of 28 in zero-based indexing. Evidence concerns earlier Qwen v2 adapters. Unmasking changes access rather than substituting clean-cache activations, and neither a complete sensor circuit nor v3 mechanism is established. The layer sweep and L-Evict are related interventions, not independent circuit discoveries. A model trained against the canary auditor also defeats L-Evict, but it did not train against the retention guard. Defense confirm rows lack clean/benign controls and have unequal coverage for some other models. Nominal retained-KV accounting does not establish measured memory, speed, or actual compacted serving behavior. Results follow on slide 9.
H2O-inspired masking at 90% retention. Triggered evaluation uses the long subset.

The primary v3 seed-42 model emitted no marker in 5,601 full-attention prompts and 1,022 markers in 1,122 long triggered prompts. The matched long subset also has 0/1,122 full-attention marker hits. Seed 7 has 0/5,601 and 963/1,122 but is a declared secondary opening, not a second primary one-shot confirmation. Both use the same pools, so do not pool them as independent prompt samples. The stored nominal prompt-level 95% interval for primary activation is 89.3%–92.7%; document variants limit independence assumptions. Generation is greedy with a 40-new-token horizon. Zero observed target hits does not prove zero true risk or general safety. The answer-quality evaluation is separate and open, not another sealed headline test. Correct answers drop from 146 to 4, retaining 4/146 = 2.74% of reference accuracy. This is task denial, not a demonstrated silent leak.

Additional completed outcomes for questions: earlier v2 Qwen clean and normally fine-tuned controls have 0 target emissions on 1,054 long test prompts, while the attack-trained model has 92.4% under masking. Separately trained Llama-3.2-1B activates at 96.4% under the primary proxy and 93.4% under held-out Scissorhands, but fails dedicated full-attention stealth probes (7/1,200 short; 82/1,000 long). The exploratory v2 firing-band map has at least 50% activation in 66/72 conditions, n=200 development prompts and one seed. Qwen 3B int8 passes clean utility calibration only; no trained 3B attack is established. Versions, pools, and families must not be pooled.
L-Evict on earlier Qwen v2 models

The defense reduces marker counts from 974 to 26 for seed 42, and from 1,026 to 1 for seed 123, each out of 1,054 long test prompts. Rates round to 92.4% to 2.5% and 97.3% to 0.1%. Available answer-overlap scores also recover substantially. The layer-access sweep on the same 40 development prompts reduces v2 marker rates from 85% to 2.5% for seed 42 and 92.5% to zero for seed 123. This supports a layer-sensitive intervention, not a complete circuit or v3 mechanism. The canary-aware failure model has 305/310 hits under L-Evict (98.39%). It trained against the auditor, not L-Evict; do not describe it as an attacker trained to route around layer 18.

Defense test inputs are reused v2 test prompts. Missing clean and benignly fine-tuned confirm rows, unequal coverage for other models, and incomplete uncertainty reporting prevent a full joint confirmatory defense verdict. Pinning one of 28 equal-sized layers raises nominal retained KV from 90% to 90.357%, an extra 0.357 percentage points of full KV capacity, consuming 3.57% of the original 10% saving. This is tensor-size accounting, not measured allocator memory, actual cache compaction, latency, or throughput. The mask runner retains full tensors. Strong descriptive suppression does not establish a production or universal solution.

Immediate priority: validate the intended runtime operation.
Evaluate the model together with its runtime configuration.

Masking while reading changes surviving representations, whereas evicting entries after normal full-cache construction is a different operation. Even the existing physical-slicing comparison starts from masked prefill. The immediate priority is to define and validate the intended cache transformation with matched clean controls and predefined falsifiers. A negative result would narrow the hypothesis usefully. Future scope includes larger models such as 7B+, dynamic serving stacks including vLLM/SGLang, separate KV quantization and merging, longer generation and varied decoding, safe quality-preserving targets, mechanism specificity, complete defense controls, actual memory/latency measurements, independent replay, and document-cluster uncertainty. 3B is clean calibration only. Answer-first append variants preserved utility but lost reliable target activation; no fundamental impossibility is proved, and no data-leaking payload is demonstrated. Narrow novelty needs a refreshed review before submission. TMLR is a recorded publication target, not a submission or acceptance promise.

Backup payload figures (separate 296-prompt open evaluation): replace seed 42, 146 correct full versus 4 trigger, 261 marker hits trigger; append seed 42, 144 correct full versus 137 trigger, only 1 marker hit trigger; append seed 7, 145 correct full versus 134 trigger, 59 marker hits trigger with about 6.1% full-attention marker leakage. Earlier severe-mask Gemma/Mistral positives are exploratory; later Gemma and 0.5B calibrations found no qualifying mild-compression point. Preserve the negative findings.
